Palpate the ankle distally and anteriorly to the lateral malleolus and ask if patient feels more pain. Usually, patient feels more pain on palpation.

The ankle is held in the neutral position, examiner stabilises the tibia just above the ankle and then tries to force the ankle into maximum inversion. The ROM can be measured or compared with the contralateral side. Inversion laxity suggests injury to calcaneofibular and anterior talofibular ligaments (ATFL).

Patient sits with knee flexed at 90 deg and ankle in plantarflexion of about 10 deg. The lower leg is stabilised by the examiner and forces patient's heel forward over the tibia. If positive, the talus can be felt sliding forwards and backwards. Laxity indicates tear of the ATFL.
Check if foot is everted and externally rotated
Check for widening of the medial joint space in the mortise view, check if talus is tilted, check for fracture or dislocation of the proximal fibula
Compress the leg firmly above the ankle. Test is positive if pain is felt over the syndesmosis.

X-ray imaging to confirm fracture
Rule out foot compartment syndrome
Check for the following deformities: flattened anterior arch, hallux valgus, claw toes, prominence of the metatarsal head in the soles (feels like walking on stones), presence of subcutaneous nodules
Check for osteoporosis and periarticular erosion at the metatarsophalangeal joint
Check for osteoporosis, erosion of the tarsal and ankle joints and the swelling of soft-tissues

procedures.procedure: Percussion of the tarsal tunnel. Positive if this results in a distal radiation of paraesthesia.
Place the patient's foot into dorsiflexion and eversion and hold for 5-10 seconds. Positive if patient's symptom is elicited.
Check for atrophy of the abductor hallucis
Check for arch stability

procedures.testName: Clinical Observation - Talus and Calcaneus Position
procedures.procedure: Check for the position of the talus and calcaneus

recommendedTests: Spurling's Test (Maximal Cervical Compression and Foraminal Compression Test)

procedures.testName: Spurling's Test (Maximal Cervical Compression and Foraminal Compression Test)
procedures.procedure: The neck is placed in extension, lateral flexion, and axial compression. The test is positive if pain is present and radiates to the arm.

The patient lies supine and the neck is positioned comfortably. The examiner places hand around the patient's mastoid process. The examiner then slightly flexes the patient's neck and pulls the head towards your torso. Test is positive if the symptoms reduce or are eliminated with traction.
Radiographic confirmation of disc herniation
Check if cervical rotation on the affected side is less than 60 degrees

recommendedTests: Spurling's Test (Maximal Cervical Compression and Foraminal Compression Test)

procedures.testName: Spurling's Test (Maximal Cervical Compression and Foraminal Compression Test)
procedures.procedure: The neck is placed in extension, lateral flexion, and axial compression. The test is positive if pain is present and radiates to the arm.
Check for loss of normal cervical lordosis, and degeneration
Physical examination and clinical assessment based on presenting symptoms
Check if muscle bulk in hand is normal (extreme cases may include atrophy)
Place forearm in supine position, flex elbow up till about 30 deg. Palpate MCL and apply lateral pressure (abduction). Positive test: increased laxity of MCL and pain.
Check for osteopenia, bone erosions, destruction of the radial head and widening of the sigmoid notch
Other laboratory tests as may be necessary (RF, anti-CCP, ESR, CRP)
Check for joint space narrowing, osteophyte formation, and subchondral sclerosis
Physical examination and clinical assessment based on presenting symptoms
Flexion, abduction, external rotation. If positive, indicates hip joint pathology such as OA.
Flexion, adduction, internal rotation. If positive, indicates intra-articular pathology (OA or FAI).
Examiner applies axial load while moving the hip in a circular motion. If positive, suggests hip joint degeneration (OA).
Examiner gently rolls the leg internally and externally. If positive, indicates intra-articular hip pathology.
Patient stands on one leg. If positive, indicates gluteus medius weakness associated with hip OA.
Check for joint space narrowing, osteophyte formation, and subchondral sclerosis
Patient stands on the affected leg. Positive sign = pain over the greater trochanter.
Patient resists external rotation of the hip. Positive sign = pain at the greater trochanteric region.
Patient lies on unaffected side. Examiner extends and abducts the hip, then slowly lowers the leg. Positive sign = leg remains elevated and does not drop.
Patient stands on one leg. Positive sign = pelvis drops on the contralateral side, indicating gluteal weakness.
Flexion, adduction, internal rotation. If positive, indicates femoroacetabular impingement or intra-articular pathology.
Flexion, abduction, external rotation. If positive, indicates hip joint pathology.
Apply axial load through the hip while circumducting. If positive, suggests intra-articular FAI.
Passively internally rotate the hip beyond its end range. Positive sign = pain or restricted motion suggesting FAI.
X-ray or MRI to confirm cam/pincer morphology and associated labral pathology.
Flexion, adduction, internal rotation. If positive, indicates intra-articular pathology such as labral tear.
Apply axial load while moving the hip in a circular motion. If positive, suggests labral tear.
Passively roll the hip internally and externally. Positive sign = pain suggesting intra-articular pathology.
Assess hip flexion contracture and labral conflict. Positive sign = restricted hip extension or pain.
MRI arthrogram to visualize labral tear and chondral damage.
Passively roll the hip. Positive sign = pain with motion, suggesting intra-articular pathology.
Flexion, adduction, internal rotation. If positive, indicates intra-articular pathology.
Flexion, abduction, external rotation. If positive, indicates hip joint pathology.
MRI is definitive for early AVN detection. X-ray for late-stage collapse.
Patient actively moves the hip through flexion/extension and rotation. Positive sign = palpable/audible snap over the hip.
Patient side-lying, hip abducted and extended, then lowered. Positive sign = snap over greater trochanter in IT band type.
Patient supine, hip flexed to chest, then extended. Positive sign = snap over iliopsoas tendon during extension.
Physical examination and clinical assessment based on presenting symptoms
Examiner gently moves the knee through passive flexion and extension. Severe pain with passive movement is positive.
Examiner strokes medial and lateral knee. Significant fluid accumulation suggests infection.
Elevated ESR, CRP, WBC count; identifies causative organism
May show joint swelling (early), joint destruction (late)
Detects early joint infection and soft tissue involvement
Patient seated with knee slightly flexed. Examiner applies resistance as the patient extends the knee. If positive, indicates patellofemoral joint irritation.
Patient stands on a 20 cm step and slowly lowers the contralateral heel to the ground while examiner observes knee alignment. If positive, suggests PFPS and poor lower limb control.

Patient supine with knee extended. Examiner applies gentle downward pressure on the superior pole of the patella while patient contracts the quadriceps. If positive, indicates patellofemoral joint dysfunction.
Patient supine and relaxed. Examiner gently pushes the patella laterally. If positive, indicates patellar instability.
Examiner lifts the lateral edge of the patella while stabilizing the medial edge. If positive, limited tilt or pain indicates tight lateral structures or OA changes.
Patient seated and actively flexes and extends the knee while examiner palpates the patellofemoral joint. If positive, indicates PFPS or patellofemoral joint irritation.
Patient supine with knee extended. Examiner glides the patella medially and laterally. If positive, indicates abnormal patellar tracking.
Patient supine. Examiner flexes the hip and knee fully, then rotates the tibia internally and externally while extending the knee. If positive, suggests meniscal tear.
Patient lies prone with knee flexed to 90°. Examiner applies downward pressure along the tibia while rotating it internally and externally. If positive, indicates meniscal injury.
Patient stands on one leg with knee slightly flexed (~20°). Patient rotates the body and knee internally and externally three times. If positive, indicates possible meniscal pathology.
Patient supine. Examiner fully flexes the knee and then allows it to passively extend. If positive, suggests a displaced meniscal fragment.

Patient stands with knees flexed and externally rotates both feet to test the medial meniscus; internally rotates both feet to test the lateral meniscus. If positive, pain or clicking occurs along the joint line.
Patient contracts the affected muscle against resistance at mid-range. Positive if pain is reproduced at the site.
Examiner stretches the affected muscle slowly. Positive if pain is reproduced.
Knee flexed ~30°, examiner stabilizes femur and pulls tibia anteriorly at the knee. Positive sign = soft endpoint or increased anterior tibial translation indicates ACL tear.
Knee flexed 90°, examiner pulls tibia anteriorly at the knee. Positive sign = increased anterior translation indicates ACL injury.
With pt supine, knee flexed to 30°, examiner stabilizes the femur and applies a valgus force to the knee. Positive sign = pain or gapping at the medial knee joint line indicates MCL injury.
With pt supine, knee flexed to 30°, examiner stabilizes the femur and applies a varus force to the knee. Positive sign = pain or gapping at the lateral knee joint line indicates LCL injury.
Knee flexed 90°, examiner pushes tibia posteriorly at the knee. Positive sign = posterior translation indicates PCL tear.
Hip and knee flexed 90°, examiner observes tibial plateau at the knee. Positive sign = sagging tibia compared to contralateral knee indicates PCL injury.
Patient supine with knee extended. Examiner applies downward pressure on the patella while asking the patient to contract the quadriceps. Positive sign = pain or crepitus at the patellofemoral joint.
Examiner lifts the lateral edge of the patella while stabilizing the medial edge. Positive sign = limited tilt or pain indicates tight lateral structures or OA changes.
Examiner moves the knee through full flexion and extension, palpating and listening for audible or palpable crepitus.
Check for joint space narrowing, osteophyte formation, subchondral sclerosis, and cyst formation
Patient lies supine with the knee extended. Examiner gently pushes the patella laterally. Positive sign = apprehension or pain indicating abnormal patellar tracking.
Patient lies supine, knee extended. Examiner gently displaces patella medially and laterally. Positive sign = excessive hypermobility or abnormal motion.
Lateral and axial X-rays; MRI if soft tissue assessment needed. Positive sign = subluxation/dislocation, osteochondral fractures, or MPFL tear.

recommendedTests: Patellar Compression Test (Modified for fracture screening)

procedures.procedure: Patient lies supine with both legs extended. Examiner asks the patient to lift the affected leg straight up without bending the knee. Positive sign = inability to lift the leg actively, indicating disruption of the extensor mechanism.

Patient lies supine with knee relaxed. Examiner palpates the patella gently using fingers to feel for tenderness, irregularity, or gap. Positive sign = localized severe tenderness, palpable gap, or irregularity.
Patient sits or lies supine. Examiner asks patient to actively straighten the knee from a flexed position. Positive sign = inability or severe pain during active extension.

procedures.testName: Patellar Compression Test (Modified for fracture screening)
procedures.procedure: Patient lies supine with knee extended. Examiner gently presses patella posteriorly toward femur. Positive sign = severe localized pain, suggesting patella fracture.
Imaging (X-ray – AP, Lateral, Skyline view). Positive sign = visible fracture line, displacement, or comminution.

recommendedTests: Palpation Test of Lateral Femoral Epicondyle

procedures.procedure: Patient lies supine. Examiner flexes knee to 90° and applies pressure over lateral femoral epicondyle while slowly extending the knee. Positive sign = pain at approximately 30° knee flexion.
Patient lies on unaffected side. Examiner extends and abducts the hip, then slowly lowers the leg. Positive sign = leg remains elevated and does not drop.
Patient stands and performs squat while examiner applies pressure over lateral femoral epicondyle. Positive sign = pain at approximately 30° knee flexion.
Patient lies supine at edge of table. Examiner observes hip and thigh position. Positive sign = tight lateral thigh indicating IT band tightness.

procedures.testName: Palpation Test of Lateral Femoral Epicondyle
procedures.procedure: Examiner palpates lateral femoral epicondyle with knee flexed and extended.
Patient stands on 25° decline board and performs squat. Positive sign = localized pain at inferior pole of patella.
Patient sits with knee flexed. Examiner resists knee extension. Positive sign = localized tendon pain.
Patient performs single-leg squat on decline surface. Positive sign = reproduction of localized tendon pain.
Examiner palpates inferior and superior poles of patella. Positive sign = localized tenderness at tendon insertion.
Patient performs repeated hopping on affected leg. Positive sign = localized tendon pain with loading.
Patient lies supine with knee extended. Examiner palpates 5–7 cm below medial joint line. Positive sign = localized tenderness.
Patient flexes knee while examiner applies resistance. Positive sign = pain at pes anserinus region.
Patient performs hip adduction while examiner applies resistance. Positive sign = pain at pes anserinus insertion.
Examiner passively stretches hamstrings. Positive sign = pain at pes anserinus region.

Patient lies supine. Examiner flexes knee to 90°. Patient actively extends knee while examiner internally rotates tibia. Positive sign = pain between 30°–40° knee extension relieved with external rotation.
Patient knee flexed to 90°. Examiner palpates femoral condyles. Positive sign = localized pain over femoral condyle.
Examiner strokes medial knee upward and lateral knee downward. Positive sign = fluid movement or bulge.
Positive sign = mass becomes firm in extension and softens or disappears in flexion, confirming Baker's cyst.
Patient prone or supine. Examiner palpates popliteal fossa. Positive sign = palpable fluid-filled mass.
Light source applied behind swelling. Positive sign = transillumination suggests fluid-filled cyst.
Examiner performs stroke test or bulge test. Positive sign = fluid accumulation present.

Examiner raises legs of patient up so that hip flexion is achieved while knee is extended. Test is positive if patient feels pain along the course of the sciatic nerve and below the knee when hip is between 30-70 degrees of flexion.
This is a modification of the SLR and dorsiflexion is applied at the end of the SLR. This reduces the angle where the test is positive.

procedures.procedure: Examiner raises legs of patient up so that hip flexion is achieved while knee is extended. Test is positive if patient feels pain along the course of the sciatic nerve and below the knee when hip is between 30-70 degrees of flexion.
This is a modification of the SLR and dorsiflexion is applied at the end of the SLR. This reduces the angle where the test is positive.

procedures.testName: Bowstring Test (Popliteal Compression Test / Tibial Nerve Stretch Sign)
procedures.procedure: This can be done while patient is lying in supine or sitting position. The examiner flexes the knee and applies pressure on the popliteal fossa evoking sciatica.
Check if knee jerk reflex is present
Check if ankle jerk reflex is present

Record the amount of time the patient spends on a cycle ergometer while in a neutral lumbar position and slumped position. If patient spends more time in the slumped position, a lumbar spinal stenosis is indicated.
The patient walks on a flat treadmill and the amount of time spent is recorded and compared with the amount of time while the treadmill is inclined such that patient walks in flexion.
The examiner ensures that the lumbar region is in moderate extension (10-30 deg) while standing and patient lies supine. Check if there are changes in the symptoms that the patient feels.
Check if a wide-based gait is present
Check if Trendelenburg's sign is present
Check for negative Romberg test
Check if Achilles tendon reflex is diminished

procedures.testName: Bowstring Test (Popliteal Compression Test / Tibial Nerve Stretch Sign)
procedures.procedure: This can be done while patient is lying in supine or sitting position. The examiner flexes the knee and applies pressure on the popliteal fossa evoking sciatica.
Patient is in prone position, knee is flexed and hip is extended. Reproduction of pain in anterior thigh is positive.
Patient's neck is flexed, hip flexed and the leg is extended. Pain is reproduced in this position.
Pain is reproduced on straight leg elevation for 30 seconds.
Radiographic confirmation of disc herniation
Check for tenderness in the paraspinal musculature

procedures.procedure: Check for Babinski sign and clonus to rule out upper motor neuron involvement

recommendedTests: Lateral Lumbar Flexion (Fingertip to Floor Test)

procedures.testName: Lateral Lumbar Flexion (Fingertip to Floor Test)
procedures.procedure: The patient stands with heel touching wall and feet wide apart, and back against the wall. Then the examiner measures the distance from middle finger to the floor. Then patient bends to side (lateral flexion). The distance between the middle finger and the floor is measured again. This measurement is done for both sides.

Examiner marks both posterior superior iliac spine, and a horizontal line is drawn between both marks. A second line is marked 5cm below the first line, and a third line is marked 10cm above the first line. Patient is then instructed to flex forward as if attempting to touch their toes. An increase of less than 5cm shows decreased lumbar spine range of motion, and ankylosing spondylitis.
Normal chest expansion is ≥ 5 cm
Normal distance is 0
Normal distance is < 15cm
Normal distance is > 100cm
Confirmatory test through laboratory investigations (HLA-B27, ESR, CRP)
X-ray to check for fracture location and displacement

While patient is seated, the examiner applies side flexion of the neck towards the affected side while applying axial compression. Sign is positive if the pain sensation felt in the shoulder-neck region is replicated.

Ask patient to abduct arm across range of motion actively. Scapular rhythm is disturbed, pain is aggravated between 60-120 degrees, pain is alleviated if shoulder is laterally rotated on abduction. If positive, SIS is indicated.
Stabilise the scapula with one hand and raise the unaffected side to full flexion with abduction and internal rotation passively. The test is positive when there is pain at the subacromial space.

Patient arm is placed in 90 deg of elevation at the scapular level and 90 deg flexion. Stabilise the upper arm with one hand and internally rotate with the other hand. The test is positive when pain is felt in the anterolateral aspect of the shoulder.

Elevate arm in scapular plane, extend elbow and thumb points towards floor with arm internally rotated. Patient is asked to hold the position with downward pressure from examiner. Positive sign = pain on examiner restriction indicating supraspinatus irritation.
Physical examination and clinical assessment based on presenting symptoms
Check for tenderness along the bicipital groove or on moving the biceps tendon (bicipital tendinitis can co-exist with other rotator cuff pathologies)

Patient is asked to abduct up to 90 deg, 30 deg flexion and internal rotation. Examiner stands behind patient and applies downward pressure. Positive sign: affected side is weaker than unaffected side. Positive sign suggests tear in the supraspinatus.

Patient holds arms close to body, elbow is flexed up to 90 deg of forward elevation in scapular plane. External rotation is instructed while examiner applies resistance. Lack of power on one side indicates weakness of the infraspinatus muscle.

Patient is asked to place their hand on their abdomen and move elbow forward. Patient is then asked to press hand on the abdomen. If subscapularis is torn, patient will be unable to perform movement and elbow will move backwards.
Patient lifts arm slightly from body and is asked to hold in external rotation. Positive when hand recoils to neutral position and suggests tear of infraspinatus or supraspinatus.

The examiner places the arm at 90 deg abduction, elbow at right angle and arm maximally rotated. Positive sign: arm drops from position. Suggests a tear of the infraspinatus or the posterior part of the rotator cuff.

Patient is asked to place hand on the back at the mid-lumbar spine. The clinician then lifts hand from the back and patient is asked to hold it there. Positive sign: inability to maintain hand while removed suggests subscapularis weakness.
Check X-ray to rule out asymptomatic calcification

Patient is in sitting or lying position, the examiner lifts the arm gently into abduction, external rotation and then extension. Test is positive if patient senses that humeral head is about to slip out anteriorly and body stiffens in apprehension. The test is repeated with the anterior part of shoulder protected.

Patient lies supine, arm abducted up to 90 deg. The examiner places their hands over the shoulder to set the fulcrum base. The humeral head is levered forward by extending and externally rotating arm. The patient immediately becomes apprehensive.

Patient lies supine, scapula is stabilised with one hand while the upper arm is grasped firmly with the other, and manoeuvring is done forward and backward (like a drawer). The drawer's test is positive if instability is marked.
Check for periarticular erosions, subchondral sclerosis, and resorption
Check for distortion of the joint, subchondral sclerosis, osteophyte formation, and narrowing of articular space
Physical examination and clinical assessment based on presenting symptoms
Patient flexes wrists fully and holds position. If positive, indicates CTS.
Examiner taps over carpal tunnel. If positive, indicates CTS.
Examiner applies direct pressure over carpal tunnel. If positive, indicates CTS.

recommendedTests: WHAT Test (Wrist Hyperflexion Abduction of Thumb)

procedures.procedure: Patient makes a fist with thumb inside fingers. Examiner ulnar deviates wrist. If positive, indicates De Quervain's.

procedures.testName: WHAT Test (Wrist Hyperflexion Abduction of Thumb)
procedures.procedure: Patient hyperflexes wrist and abducts thumb against resistance. If positive, indicates De Quervain's.
Examiner applies stress to specific ligaments. Positive sign = pain or instability localized to the injured ligament.
Rule out undisplaced fracture or other bony injury
Wrist in ulnar deviation + axial load + rotation. Positive if ulnar wrist pain.
Patient pushes up from chair using hands. Positive if ulnar wrist pain.
MRI or arthrogram to assess TFCC complex integrity
Light is applied through the swelling. Positive sign = transillumination confirms fluid-filled cyst.
Patient extends wrist against resistance. Positive sign = pain 4–6 cm proximal to the wrist in the dorsal radial forearm.
Palpation of anatomical snuffbox. If positive, indicates scaphoid fracture.
Axial load applied through thumb. If positive, indicates scaphoid fracture.
X-ray and/or MRI to confirm scaphoid fracture, especially if initial X-ray is normal.
Apply compression through wrist. Positive if central dorsal wrist pain.
X-ray for staging, MRI for early AVN detection.
